sla_notes_intro: Fine Art is the branch of art concerned with creating works valued primarily for their beauty and expressive meaning, such as drawing, painting, sculpture and printmaking.
sla_notes_details: The meaning of Fine Art covers visual works created mainly for aesthetic and expressive purposes rather than pure utility. Its principles include balance, contrast, emphasis, rhythm, proportion, unity and harmony, which guide artists in arranging elements such as line, shape, colour, texture and space into a pleasing composition. Fine Art has several forms including drawing, painting, sculpture, printmaking and ceramics, and it performs functions such as communication, decoration, documentation of history and culture, and generation of income. It relates to other disciplines such as History (recording past events through images), Geography (mapping and landscape depiction), and Mathematics (proportion and geometry in composition).
sla_notes_illustrations: A student who arranges a still life of fruits using balance and contrast of colour is applying the principles of Fine Art to create a pleasing composition.
sla_notes_daily_life: Fine Art skills are used daily in sign writing for local shops, designing kitenge patterns and decorating houses for ceremonies.
sla_exercise: State two principles of Fine Art.::Balance and contrast are two principles of Fine Art.||Name one function of Fine Art in society.::Fine Art communicates ideas and messages to the community.||Explain the relationship between Fine Art and History.::Fine Art records and preserves historical events and culture through images and artefacts.

sla_references: TET(2023), FINE ART SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM I-IV, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Every branch of Fine Art has basic fundamentals that a learner must master before creating advanced works.
sla_notes_details: The fundamentals of drawing include mastering line quality, shading, proportion and perspective to represent objects accurately. Painting fundamentals include colour mixing, brush control, and application of colour in layers (washes) to build tone and depth. Printmaking fundamentals include preparing a printing surface (plate, block or stencil), applying ink evenly, and transferring the image onto a receiving surface such as paper or fabric through pressure. These fundamentals form the foundation on which more advanced techniques in each discipline are built.
sla_notes_illustrations: A learner practising straight and curved lines with a pencil before attempting a portrait is building the fundamental drawing skill of line control.
sla_notes_daily_life: Sign writers and tailors use fundamentals of drawing and colour mixing daily when designing advertisements and printing fabric patterns.
sla_exercise: Name one fundamental skill needed in drawing.::Line quality or shading control is a fundamental skill in drawing.||What is a printing plate used for?::It is the surface prepared to carry an image that is transferred onto paper or fabric.||Why is colour mixing important in painting?::It allows the artist to produce the exact tone and shade needed for the artwork.

sla_notes_intro: Fine Art in Tanzania has developed through distinct historical and stylistic trends reflecting the country's culture and history.
sla_notes_details: Traditional Tanzanian art trends include rock art of hunter-gatherer communities such as the Sandawe, wood carving traditions of the Makonde people known for Shetani and Ujamaa sculptures, and Tingatinga painting which uses bright flat colours to depict animals and daily life. Other trends include basketry, pottery and body decoration practised by various ethnic groups. These trends show characteristics such as symbolism, use of locally available materials, and communication of social and spiritual values. Contemporary Tanzanian art has grown from these roots while incorporating modern themes and materials.
sla_notes_illustrations: A Makonde carver producing an Ujamaa sculpture of interlocked human figures is continuing a distinct Tanzanian art trend that symbolises family unity.
sla_notes_daily_life: Tingatinga paintings are sold to tourists in Dar es Salaam markets, generating income while promoting Tanzanian culture internationally.
sla_exercise: Name one traditional Tanzanian art trend.::Makonde wood carving or Tingatinga painting is a traditional Tanzanian art trend.||What does an Ujamaa sculpture symbolise?::It symbolises family unity and togetherness.||Which community is known for Tingatinga painting?::Tingatinga painting originated with artists from the Tingatinga family near Dar es Salaam.

sla_notes_intro: Decorative drawings are drawings created purely to enhance the visual appeal of an object or surface using patterns and motifs.
sla_notes_details: Creating simple decorative drawings involves selecting a theme or motif, such as geometric shapes, plants or animals, and repeating or arranging it in a pattern using techniques such as tessellation, symmetry and border design. Tools used include pencils, rulers and drawing paper. The process begins with sketching light guidelines, developing the motif, then finalising with clean outlines and shading to enhance depth. Decorative drawings can be applied to borders of books, textile designs or wall decorations.
sla_notes_illustrations: A student drawing a repeated triangular pattern along the border of a greeting card is creating a simple decorative drawing.
sla_notes_daily_life: Decorative drawings are used to design invitation cards, kanga borders and classroom charts.

sla_notes_intro: Decorative paintings apply colour to patterns and motifs to beautify a surface or object.
sla_notes_details: The process of creating simple decorative paintings starts with planning a motif, sketching it lightly on the surface, then applying colour using brushes, sponges or fingers depending on the desired texture. Artists consider colour harmony, choosing complementary or analogous colours to make the pattern visually appealing. Layering colours from light to dark builds depth, and a clear outline can be added last to sharpen the pattern. Common surfaces for decorative painting include paper, wood, walls and fabric.
sla_notes_illustrations: A student painting a border of colourful flowers around a classroom noticeboard is creating a decorative painting using colour harmony.
sla_notes_daily_life: House walls and calabashes in many Tanzanian communities are decorated with painted patterns during festivals and ceremonies.

sla_notes_intro: A monoprint is a unique print made by transferring an image from a prepared surface onto paper, producing only one copy.
sla_notes_details: To create a simple decorative monoprint, the artist applies ink or paint onto a smooth surface such as glass, plastic or a tile, then either draws into the wet ink with a tool to remove parts of it, or places objects/leaves onto the inked surface to create texture. A sheet of paper is then pressed firmly onto the inked surface and peeled off carefully to reveal the printed pattern. Because the ink shifts each time, no two monoprints are exactly alike, making the technique valuable for producing unique decorative patterns.
sla_notes_illustrations: A student pressing a leaf onto an inked glass sheet and then printing it onto paper produces a unique decorative monoprint of the leaf's texture.
sla_notes_daily_life: Monoprinting techniques are used by local artisans to create unique greeting cards and decorative wrapping paper for sale.
sla_exercise: What is a monoprint?::It is a unique print made by transferring an image from a prepared surface onto paper.||Name one surface used to prepare ink for monoprinting.::Glass, plastic or a tile can be used to prepare ink for monoprinting.||Why is each monoprint unique?::Because the ink shifts differently each time a print is pulled, so no two prints are identical.

sla_notes_intro: Charcoal is a traditional drawing medium made from burnt wood, valued for its rich dark tones and blending qualities.
sla_notes_details: To draw with charcoal, the artist first sketches the basic outline lightly, then builds up tone by applying charcoal in layers, using the side of the stick for broad shading and the tip for fine detail. Blending tools such as tissue, cotton or a finger are used to soften transitions between light and dark areas. An eraser can be used to lift charcoal and create highlights. Fixative spray or a similar substance can be applied at the end to prevent smudging of the finished drawing.
sla_notes_illustrations: A student shading the dark background of a portrait with the side of a charcoal stick, then lifting highlights with an eraser, demonstrates basic charcoal drawing technique.
sla_notes_daily_life: Charcoal, being locally available from burnt firewood, is an affordable drawing material used by many students and artists in rural areas.

sla_notes_intro: Natural pigments can be obtained from plants, soil and minerals in the local environment to create paint for artwork.
sla_notes_details: Colours from the surrounding environment are obtained by crushing or grinding materials such as coloured soils (ochre for reds and browns), charcoal (for black), chalk or lime (for white), and plant materials such as leaves and flowers (for greens and yellows). These materials are usually mixed with a binder such as water, egg or plant sap to make them adhere to a surface. The artist then applies the natural paint using fingers, brushes made from twigs, or sponges to create the artwork, connecting the work directly to locally available resources.
sla_notes_illustrations: A student grinding red ochre soil and mixing it with water to paint a pattern on paper is using colours from the surrounding environment.
sla_notes_daily_life: Communities without access to manufactured paints traditionally decorate houses and pottery using natural pigments from local soil and plants.

sla_notes_intro: Fine Art activities produce waste materials such as used paper, empty paint containers, broken tools and leftover chemicals that must be disposed of safely.
sla_notes_details: Proper disposal methods include separating waste into categories such as biodegradable (paper, plant offcuts) and non-biodegradable (plastic containers, metal tools) for appropriate handling. Biodegradable waste can be composted, while non-biodegradable waste should be collected for recycling where facilities exist or disposed of in designated bins. Hazardous materials such as leftover solvents or old paint should never be poured into water sources or soil, as they can pollute the environment; instead they should be sealed and taken to appropriate collection points. Occupational health practices also include wearing gloves and washing hands after handling waste materials.
sla_notes_illustrations: A student separating used paper for composting from empty paint tins for recycling collection is practising correct waste disposal from Fine Art activities.
sla_notes_daily_life: Proper disposal of art waste protects local rivers and soil from pollution caused by paints and chemicals in the community.
sla_exercise: Name one type of waste produced in Fine Art activities.::Used paper or empty paint containers are waste produced in Fine Art activities.||Why should leftover paint not be poured into water sources?::Because it can pollute the water and harm the environment and living things.||State one safe practice when handling art waste.::Wearing gloves when handling waste materials is a safe practice.

sla_notes_intro: Still life composition is the arrangement of inanimate objects, such as fruits, bottles and cloth, into a pleasing visual grouping for drawing or painting.
sla_notes_details: Basic tenets of still life composition include selecting objects of varying size, shape and texture, arranging them to create a focal point, and considering negative space (the empty area around objects). Objects are usually grouped in odd numbers to avoid symmetry that looks too rigid, and overlapping objects creates a sense of depth. Lighting is arranged from one direction to create clear highlights and shadows that define the form of each object. The artist studies the composition from a fixed viewpoint before starting to draw or paint.
sla_notes_illustrations: A student arranging three mangoes, a bottle and a cloth on a table with light coming from one window is applying the tenets of still life composition before sketching them.
sla_notes_daily_life: Shopkeepers arranging fruits and goods attractively on display tables use similar principles of composition to still life arrangement to attract customers.
sla_exercise: What is still life composition?::It is the arrangement of inanimate objects into a pleasing grouping for drawing or painting.||Why are objects often arranged in odd numbers in still life?::Odd numbers avoid a rigid, overly symmetrical appearance.||What is negative space in a composition?::It is the empty area surrounding the objects in the arrangement.

sla_notes_intro: Art theories help explain why and how artworks are valued, with formalism and functionalism offering two different perspectives.
sla_notes_details: Formalism is the theory that the value of an artwork lies in its formal visual qualities, such as line, colour, shape, balance and composition, rather than in its subject matter or purpose. A formalist judges a sculpture by how well its shapes and proportions work together. Functionalism, on the other hand, holds that the value of an artwork lies in its usefulness and the purpose it serves in society, such as a decorated pot that is both beautiful and useful for storing water. Understanding both theories helps an artist balance aesthetic quality with practical purpose when creating works.
sla_notes_illustrations: A critic praising a woven basket purely for its symmetrical pattern is applying formalism, while a critic praising the same basket for how well it carries water is applying functionalism.
sla_notes_daily_life: Furniture makers apply functionalism by ensuring a decorated chair is both attractive and comfortable to sit on.
sla_exercise: What does formalism emphasise in judging art?::It emphasises formal visual qualities such as line, colour and composition.||What does functionalism emphasise in judging art?::It emphasises the usefulness and purpose the artwork serves.||Give an example of an object that can be judged by both theories.::A decorated clay pot can be judged for its beauty (formalism) and its usefulness for storing water (functionalism).

sla_notes_intro: Functional drawings are drawings created to serve a practical purpose, such as illustrating how an object works or is constructed.
sla_notes_details: Creating a functional drawing begins with identifying the object's purpose and the information it must communicate, such as dimensions, parts or assembly order. The artist uses accurate measurement, straight lines and labelling to ensure clarity, often including different views (front, side, top) of the object. Unlike purely decorative drawing, functional drawing prioritises accuracy and communication over aesthetic embellishment, though neatness and clear presentation remain important.
sla_notes_illustrations: A student drawing a labelled diagram of a simple wooden stool showing its measurements and joints is creating a functional drawing.
sla_notes_daily_life: Carpenters and technicians use functional drawings to plan and construct furniture and equipment accurately.

sla_notes_intro: Functional paintings combine visual appeal with a practical purpose, such as painted signage or safety markings.
sla_notes_details: To create a functional painting, the artist first identifies the message or purpose it must serve, such as directing people, advertising a product or protecting a surface. Bold, clear colours and simple legible designs are chosen to ensure the message is understood quickly, and durable paint suited to the surface and environment is selected. The composition balances attractiveness with clarity, avoiding excessive detail that could confuse the intended message.
sla_notes_illustrations: A student painting a simple road-safety sign with bold red and white colours for a school project is creating a functional painting meant to communicate a clear message.

sla_notes_intro: Pastels are sticks of pigment that allow direct, vibrant colour application similar to painting but with the convenience of a drawing medium.
sla_notes_details: To draw using pastels, the artist applies colour directly onto textured paper suited to holding pigment, building up layers from light to dark or blending colours together using fingers or a blending stump. Techniques include hatching (parallel strokes), layering complementary colours for vibrancy, and using the side of the pastel stick for broad areas of colour. Because pastel can smudge easily, careful handling and fixative spray help preserve the finished artwork.
sla_notes_illustrations: A student blending orange and yellow pastel strokes with a finger to create a smooth sunset gradient is using basic pastel drawing technique.
sla_notes_daily_life: Local artists use pastel drawing to quickly produce vibrant portraits and landscapes for sale at markets and cultural events.

sla_notes_intro: Water colours, acrylics and oil paints are three common painting media, each with distinct properties and techniques of application.
sla_notes_details: Water colours are transparent and diluted with water, applied in thin washes that allow the white of the paper to show through for highlights; they dry quickly and are best for light, luminous effects. Acrylics are fast-drying, water-based paints that can be applied thickly or thinly and are versatile for both detailed and bold work; they remain flexible once dry. Oil paints are slow-drying, mixed with oil-based mediums, and allow blending of colours directly on the canvas over an extended working time, producing rich, deep tones. The choice of medium depends on the desired effect, drying time available, and surface being painted.
sla_notes_illustrations: A student using thin water colour washes to paint a soft, glowing sky, then switching to acrylics for the bold foreground shapes, is applying the properties of each medium appropriately.
sla_notes_daily_life: Professional artists choose oil paints for artworks that need extended working time and rich blending, while sign painters often prefer fast-drying acrylics.

sla_notes_intro: Perspective composition creates the illusion of depth and distance on a flat surface, making objects appear three-dimensional.
sla_notes_details: Basic tenets of perspective include the horizon line (representing eye level), vanishing points (where parallel lines appear to converge), and the rule that objects appear smaller and closer together as they recede into the distance. One-point perspective uses a single vanishing point, suitable for objects facing the viewer directly, such as a road disappearing into the distance, while two-point perspective uses two vanishing points for objects viewed at an angle, such as the corner of a building. Overlapping, size variation and placement higher on the page also help suggest depth.
sla_notes_illustrations: A student drawing a straight road that narrows towards a single point on the horizon is applying one-point perspective to create the illusion of distance.
sla_notes_daily_life: Architects and building designers use perspective drawing to show clients how a proposed building will look from different viewpoints.
sla_exercise: What is a vanishing point in perspective drawing?::It is the point where parallel lines appear to converge in the distance.||What is the horizon line?::It represents the viewer's eye level in a perspective drawing.||Name one technique, besides vanishing points, used to suggest depth.::Overlapping objects or reducing their size suggests depth.

sla_notes_intro: These theories explain different reasons why an artwork can be considered valuable or successful.
sla_notes_details: Imitationalism (also called representationalism) holds that an artwork's value lies in how accurately it imitates or represents reality, judging success by realism and technical skill in capturing appearance. Emotionalism holds that an artwork's value lies in its ability to communicate and evoke feeling or emotion in the viewer, even if it is not realistic, valuing expressive colour, form and content over accuracy. A highly realistic portrait would be praised under imitationalism, while an expressive, distorted painting that conveys strong sadness would be praised under emotionalism.
sla_notes_illustrations: A judge who scores a drawing highly because every detail of the model's face is accurately captured is applying imitationalism, while a judge who scores an abstract painting highly because it evokes strong emotion is applying emotionalism.
sla_notes_daily_life: Local mural artists sometimes use exaggerated, emotional imagery rather than realistic detail to communicate strong social messages to the community.

sla_notes_intro: Perspective drawing applies the tenets of vanishing points and horizon lines to create realistic three-dimensional scenes on paper.
sla_notes_details: To create a perspective drawing, the artist first draws a horizon line and marks one or two vanishing points depending on the chosen perspective type. Guidelines are drawn lightly from the vanishing points to establish the direction of receding edges, such as the sides of a road or building. The main shapes of the scene are then constructed along these guidelines before adding details, shading and removing the construction lines. Practising with simple subjects such as a row of buildings or a hallway helps build confidence before attempting complex scenes.
sla_notes_illustrations: A student constructing a drawing of a classroom corridor using two vanishing points to show the receding walls and ceiling is creating a perspective drawing.
sla_notes_daily_life: Interior designers create perspective drawings to show clients how a renovated room will appear before construction begins.
sla_exercise: What is the first step in creating a perspective drawing?::Drawing a horizon line and marking the vanishing point(s).||Why are guidelines drawn lightly at first?::So they can be erased later without damaging the final drawing.||Name one subject suitable for practising perspective drawing.::A row of buildings or a hallway is suitable for practising perspective drawing.

sla_notes_intro: Perspective painting combines the illusion of depth with colour and tone to produce a convincing three-dimensional scene.
sla_notes_details: In addition to using vanishing points and horizon lines, perspective painting uses atmospheric perspective, where distant objects are painted with lighter, cooler and less detailed colours, while closer objects have warmer, more saturated colours and sharper detail. This mimics how the atmosphere affects our perception of distant objects. The artist blocks in the main colour areas first, following the perspective guidelines, before refining details and adjusting tones to strengthen the sense of depth.
sla_notes_illustrations: A student painting distant hills in pale blue-grey while painting the foreground trees in vivid green demonstrates atmospheric perspective in a perspective painting.
sla_notes_daily_life: Landscape painters selling artwork to tourists use perspective and atmospheric colour techniques to make scenic paintings of Tanzanian landscapes appear realistic and appealing.
sla_exercise: What is atmospheric perspective?::It is the technique of using lighter, cooler colours for distant objects to suggest depth.||Which colours are typically used for objects in the foreground?::Warmer, more saturated colours with sharper detail are used for foreground objects.||Why does atmospheric perspective make a painting look more realistic?::It mimics how the atmosphere naturally affects our perception of distant objects.

sla_notes_intro: Relief printing involves carving away the non-printing areas of a block so that the raised surface holds ink and transfers the design onto paper or fabric.
sla_notes_details: To create a relief print, the artist first sketches the design onto a printing block, such as a linoleum or wood block, then carves away the areas that should remain white, leaving the design raised. Ink is rolled evenly onto the raised surface using a brayer, and paper is pressed firmly onto the inked block, then peeled away to reveal the print. Multiple identical prints can be made from a single block, making relief printing suitable for both decorative patterns and functional items such as labelled illustrations or repeated fabric motifs.
sla_notes_illustrations: A student carving a simple leaf motif into a linoleum block and printing it repeatedly to decorate wrapping paper is creating a decorative relief print.
sla_notes_daily_life: Local artisans use relief printing to produce multiple copies of fabric patterns for sale, making production faster than hand-painting each piece.
sla_exercise: What tool is used to carve a relief printing block?::A carving or cutting knife is used to carve the block.||What is a brayer used for in relief printing?::It is used to roll ink evenly onto the raised surface of the block.||Why is relief printing suitable for producing multiple copies?::Because the same carved block can be inked and pressed repeatedly to produce identical prints.

sla_notes_intro: Collage is a technique of creating an artwork by assembling different materials, such as paper, fabric or photographs, onto a surface.
sla_notes_details: To create a contemporary drawing by collaging, the artist selects varied materials such as newspaper cuttings, coloured paper, fabric scraps or found objects, then arranges and glues them onto a background to build an image, often combined with drawn lines or shading to unify the composition. Layering materials of different textures and colours creates visual interest and can convey contemporary themes such as social issues or urban life in a way that traditional drawing alone cannot easily achieve.

sla_notes_intro: Collage painting combines painted areas with glued materials to produce a mixed-media contemporary artwork.
sla_notes_details: In collage painting, the artist alternates between gluing pieces of paper, fabric or other flat materials and painting over or around them to blend the collaged elements into a unified composition. Acrylic paint or glue-based mediums work well since they bond materials securely while allowing further painting on top. This mixed-media approach allows textures from the glued materials to remain visible through or beside painted areas, adding depth and tactile interest that pure painting cannot achieve alone.
sla_notes_illustrations: A student gluing pieces of kitenge fabric onto a canvas and then painting a figure around them to blend the fabric pattern into the artwork's clothing is creating a contemporary collage painting.

sla_notes_intro: Realistic drawing aims to represent a subject as accurately as possible in proportion, tone and detail on a flat surface.
sla_notes_details: To create a realistic two-dimensional drawing, the artist observes the subject carefully, measuring proportions using techniques such as comparing the size of different parts against each other. Light and shadow are studied to determine where to apply shading, using a full range of tones from highlights to deep shadows to suggest form. Fine details such as texture (e.g. skin, fabric or fur) are added last, once the overall proportion and tonal structure are correct, ensuring the drawing closely resembles the real subject.
sla_notes_illustrations: A student carefully measuring the proportions of a friend's face before shading it with a full range of tones to make it resemble a photograph is creating a realistic two-dimensional drawing.
sla_notes_daily_life: Portrait artists at cultural events create realistic drawings of customers as a form of income-generating art service.
sla_exercise: What is the goal of realistic two-dimensional drawing?::To represent a subject as accurately as possible on a flat surface.||Why is measuring proportion important in realistic drawing?::It ensures that the different parts of the subject are correctly sized relative to each other.||What is added last in a realistic drawing?::Fine details such as texture are added last, after proportion and tone are established.

sla_notes_intro: Realistic painting applies careful colour mixing and tonal control to represent a subject as it appears in real life.
sla_notes_details: To create a realistic two-dimensional painting, the artist mixes colours to match the exact hues observed in the subject, paying close attention to how light affects colour, such as warmer tones in direct light and cooler tones in shadow. Layering thin glazes of paint can build up realistic skin tones or textures gradually. Edges are softened or sharpened depending on focus, with the main subject usually rendered with the sharpest detail and highest contrast to draw the viewer's eye.
sla_notes_illustrations: A student mixing several shades of brown and pink to accurately match the skin tone of a model under classroom lighting is practising realistic painting technique.
sla_notes_daily_life: Portrait and landscape painters selling artwork to the public rely on realistic painting skills to produce work that clients recognise and value.

sla_notes_intro: Ethics in Fine Art concern the moral responsibilities artists have towards originality, other people's work, and the subjects they depict.
sla_notes_details: Basic ethical norms include originality, meaning an artist should create their own work rather than copying another artist's work and presenting it as their own (plagiarism). Artists should also respect the dignity of the people or cultures they depict, avoiding demeaning or disrespectful portrayals, and should obtain consent when creating a portrait or using someone's image. Honesty in representing materials and techniques used, and giving credit when inspired by another artist's style or when collaborating, are also important ethical values that maintain trust and respect within the art community.
sla_notes_illustrations: A student who paints a scene inspired by a famous artist's style but openly acknowledges the inspiration, rather than claiming the idea as entirely original, is observing an ethical norm.
sla_notes_daily_life: Professional artists exhibiting work in galleries are expected to disclose whether a piece is an original creation or a reproduction to maintain trust with buyers.
sla_exercise: What is plagiarism in the context of art?::It is copying another artist's work and presenting it as one's own.||Why is consent important when creating a portrait of someone?::It respects the dignity and rights of the person being depicted.||Name one ethical value an artist should uphold.::Originality or honesty about materials and techniques used.

sla_notes_intro: Copyright law protects an artist's original work from being copied, distributed or used by others without permission.
sla_notes_details: In Tanzania, copyright protection for artistic works is governed under the Copyright and Neighbouring Rights Act, which automatically grants the creator of an original artwork exclusive rights to reproduce, distribute, exhibit and adapt the work upon its creation, without requiring formal registration, although registration can provide additional evidence of ownership. Copyright generally protects the artist's rights for their lifetime plus a set number of years afterward, allowing heirs to benefit. Unauthorised reproduction or commercial use of an artist's work without permission is an infringement that can lead to legal consequences.
sla_notes_illustrations: A photographer who uses a local painter's artwork on t-shirts for sale without asking permission is infringing the painter's copyright under Tanzanian law.
sla_notes_daily_life: Understanding copyright helps young Tanzanian artists protect their designs when selling artwork online or to local businesses.
sla_exercise: What law governs copyright of artworks in Tanzania?::The Copyright and Neighbouring Rights Act governs copyright of artworks in Tanzania.||Does an artist need to register their work to be protected by copyright?::No, copyright protection is automatic upon creation of an original work, though registration can help as evidence.||What happens if someone uses an artist's work without permission?::It is copyright infringement, which can lead to legal consequences.

sla_notes_intro: Although copyright exists automatically, artists in Tanzania can formally register their works for additional legal protection and proof of ownership.
sla_notes_details: The registration process involves submitting an application, along with copies or samples of the artwork and relevant details such as the artist's name, title of the work and date of creation, to the responsible government body such as the Copyright Society of Tanzania (COSOTA). A registration fee is usually paid, and once processed, the artist receives a certificate of registration that serves as official evidence of ownership and the date of creation, which is valuable if a dispute over originality or ownership arises later.
sla_notes_illustrations: An artist submitting a painting's photograph, title and personal details to COSOTA and receiving a registration certificate is completing the artwork registration process.
sla_notes_daily_life: Registering artwork gives Tanzanian artists stronger legal standing if their designs are used commercially by another party without permission.

sla_notes_intro: Marketing strategies help artists sell their work successfully by reaching the right customers with an appealing offer.
sla_notes_details: Basic marketing strategies for artworks follow the four Ps: product (ensuring the artwork is well finished, presented and meets buyer needs), promotion (advertising through social media, exhibitions, word of mouth and local markets to reach potential buyers), price (setting a fair price that reflects the materials, time and skill invested while remaining competitive), and place (choosing where to sell, such as galleries, online platforms, markets or direct commissions, based on where target customers are found). Combining these four elements effectively increases an artist's chances of selling their work.
sla_notes_illustrations: A student who prices a finished painting fairly, posts photos of it on social media, and sells it at a local cultural exhibition is applying the four marketing strategies of product, price, promotion and place.
sla_notes_daily_life: Local artists increasingly use social media platforms such as Instagram and WhatsApp to promote and sell their artworks directly to customers.

sla_notes_intro: Pictorial composition refers to the arrangement of all visual elements within a picture to create a unified, complete scene, usually involving multiple objects or figures in a setting.
sla_notes_details: Basic tenets of pictorial composition include establishing a clear focal point that draws the viewer's attention first, arranging supporting elements to guide the eye through the picture using compositional devices such as leading lines, the rule of thirds, and framing. Balance is achieved by distributing visual weight (through size, colour and placement) across the picture, while unity is achieved by relating all elements through consistent style, colour palette or theme. Foreground, middle ground and background are considered together to build a complete, believable pictorial scene, unlike a simple still life or single-object study.
sla_notes_illustrations: A student arranging a village scene with a hut in the middle ground, people in the foreground and mountains in the background, all connected by a winding path, is applying the tenets of pictorial composition.
sla_notes_daily_life: Muralists painting scenes on the walls of community buildings apply pictorial composition to create balanced, meaningful scenes that tell a story to viewers.
sla_exercise: What is a focal point in a pictorial composition?::It is the main element that draws the viewer's attention first.||Name one compositional device used to guide the viewer's eye.::Leading lines or the rule of thirds guide the viewer's eye.||Why is unity important in a pictorial composition?::It relates all elements together through consistent style, colour or theme, making the picture feel complete.

sla_notes_intro: This activity applies the tenets of pictorial composition specifically to the medium of drawing, producing a complete, multi-element scene.
sla_notes_details: To create a drawing from a pictorial composition, the artist first plans a thumbnail sketch to test the arrangement of the focal point, supporting elements and depth (foreground, middle ground, background) before committing to the final paper. Guidelines for perspective and proportion are established, then the main shapes are blocked in lightly. Details and tonal shading are added progressively from background to foreground, ensuring the focal point receives the most contrast and detail to draw attention, consistent with the planned composition.
sla_notes_illustrations: A student sketching several thumbnail versions of a marketplace scene before choosing the best arrangement and developing it into a final detailed drawing is following the process of pictorial composition drawing.
sla_notes_daily_life: Illustrators for children's storybooks use pictorial composition drawing skills to create scenes that clearly tell a story at a glance.

sla_notes_intro: This activity extends pictorial composition into painting, using colour and tone in addition to arrangement to build a complete scene.
sla_notes_details: In painting a pictorial composition, the artist uses colour temperature and value to reinforce depth, with warmer, more saturated colours and stronger contrast typically used in the foreground and focal point, while cooler, less saturated colours recede into the background. The painting is usually built up in stages, starting with a rough colour block-in of all major shapes and grounds, then refining values and details, working from large areas to small, and from background to foreground, to maintain overall unity and balance throughout the process.
sla_notes_illustrations: A student blocking in a warm orange sunset sky first, then adding cooler blue hills in the background and a strongly contrasted, detailed hut in the foreground, is painting a pictorial composition with depth.
sla_notes_daily_life: Landscape and scene painters selling work at cultural centres use pictorial composition painting to create appealing, story-telling artworks that attract buyers.
sla_exercise: Which colours are typically used for the foreground in a pictorial composition painting?::Warmer, more saturated colours with stronger contrast are used for the foreground.||In what order is a pictorial composition painting usually built up?::From large areas to small details, and from background to foreground.||Why is colour temperature used to reinforce depth?::Because warm colours appear to advance and cool colours appear to recede, supporting the illusion of distance.

sla_notes_intro: This activity applies printmaking techniques, both monoprint and relief methods, to reproduce a full pictorial scene rather than a simple motif.
sla_notes_details: To create a monoprint or relief print of a pictorial composition, the artist first designs the full scene, considering how the printmaking process will simplify tonal and colour ranges compared to drawing or painting. For a monoprint, ink is applied in varying amounts across the plate to represent different grounds before a single impression is pulled. For a relief print, the composition is carved in layers of depth, sometimes using multiple blocks or multiple print passes to build up colour and tone for a more complex pictorial scene, requiring careful planning of registration so each layer aligns correctly.
sla_notes_illustrations: A student carving a village scene relief block in stages, printing the background layer first, then aligning and printing a second block for the foreground details in a different colour, is creating a multi-layer relief print of a pictorial composition.
sla_notes_daily_life: Textile printing workshops use multi-block relief printing to reproduce complex pictorial scenes on fabric for sale in local markets.

sla_notes_intro: Digital drawing uses electronic devices and software instead of traditional materials to produce artwork.
sla_notes_details: Simple digital drawing involves using a device such as a computer, tablet or smartphone with drawing software (such as free apps like Autodesk Sketchbook or built-in paint programs) and an input tool such as a stylus, mouse or touchscreen. The artist selects digital brushes that mimic traditional tools such as pencils or pens, works in layers that can be edited independently, and can easily undo mistakes, unlike traditional media. Basic digital drawing skills include line work, shading using digital brush opacity, and organising work using layers for backgrounds, line art and colour separately.
sla_notes_illustrations: A student using a tablet and stylus to sketch a portrait in a drawing app, placing the line art and shading on separate layers, is creating a simple digital drawing.
sla_notes_daily_life: Graphic designers and social media content creators use digital drawing skills to produce illustrations and logos for local businesses.

sla_notes_intro: Digital painting applies colour electronically using software, simulating traditional painting techniques with added digital flexibility.
sla_notes_details: In simple digital painting, the artist uses a digital brush tool with adjustable size, opacity and blending settings to apply colour onto a digital canvas, often building the painting in layers for background, midground and foreground elements that can be adjusted independently. Digital colour mixing can be done using a colour picker tool for precise colour matching, and blending modes can simulate effects such as glazing or lighting changes that would take much longer with traditional paint. sla_notes_daily_life: Freelance digital artists earn income by creating digital paintings and illustrations for clients through online platforms.

sla_notes_intro: Three-dimensional drawing uses techniques that make a two-dimensional surface represent depth, volume and solidity, as if an object or figure occupies real space.
sla_notes_details: Realistic three-dimensional drawing relies on understanding how light falls on a form, dividing it into distinct areas: highlight, light, halftone, core shadow, reflected light and cast shadow. Correct proportion and foreshortening (adjusting the apparent length of a form seen at an angle) are essential to convincingly represent volume. Cross-contour lines can help the artist visualise the surface curving in space before shading is applied. Careful blending of tones between these areas gives the illusion that the drawn object has real, solid form rather than appearing flat.
sla_notes_illustrations: A student shading a drawn sphere with a distinct highlight, gradual mid-tones, a core shadow band and a soft cast shadow beneath it is creating a realistic three-dimensional drawing.
sla_notes_daily_life: Product designers create realistic three-dimensional drawings of proposed items, such as furniture or packaging, to present convincing concepts to clients before production.
sla_exercise: Name one of the tonal areas used to show three-dimensional form.::Highlight, core shadow or cast shadow is one of the tonal areas used.||What is foreshortening?::It is adjusting the apparent length of a form as seen from an angle to convey depth.||Why are cross-contour lines useful before shading?::They help the artist visualise how the surface curves in space.

sla_notes_intro: This activity extends realistic three-dimensional rendering into painting, using colour alongside tone to convincingly represent volume and form.
sla_notes_details: In realistic three-dimensional painting, the artist applies the same principles of light and shadow used in drawing, but must also manage how colour temperature shifts across a form, with warmer tones typically in areas of direct light and cooler tones in shadow areas, especially where reflected light or ambient colour is present. Careful blending of paint, whether through wet-on-wet techniques or glazing thin layers, achieves smooth transitions between tonal areas that suggest a rounded, solid form rather than a flat, painted shape.
sla_notes_illustrations: A student painting an apple with warm reddish-orange tones on the lit side and cooler, slightly purple shadow tones on the shaded side, blended smoothly between them, is creating a realistic three-dimensional painting.
sla_notes_daily_life: Portrait and still-life painters rely on three-dimensional painting skills to produce lifelike artworks that are valued and purchased by clients.
sla_exercise: What colour shift typically occurs from the lit side to the shadow side of a form?::Colours typically shift from warmer in the light to cooler in the shadow.||Name one blending technique used in realistic painting.::Wet-on-wet blending or glazing thin layers is used.||Why is smooth tonal transition important in three-dimensional painting?::It suggests a rounded, solid form rather than a flat shape.

sla_teaching_aids: Relevant online resources related to the basic ethical considerations guiding the collection|Display of artworks
sla_references: TET(2023), FINE ART SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM I-IV, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Museums, galleries and collectors must follow ethical considerations when acquiring and exhibiting artworks, particularly cultural and historical pieces.
sla_notes_details: Basic ethical considerations include ensuring artworks, especially cultural artefacts, were acquired legally and with proper consent, rather than through theft or exploitation of communities. Provenance (the documented history of an artwork's ownership) should be researched and disclosed to confirm legitimate acquisition. Display should respect the cultural context and significance of the work, avoiding presentation that misrepresents or disrespects the community it came from, and where appropriate, involving source communities in decisions about how their cultural artworks are displayed or used.
sla_notes_illustrations: A gallery that researches and publicly discloses the full ownership history of a traditional Makonde sculpture before displaying it is following ethical considerations of provenance and transparency.
sla_notes_daily_life: National museums in Tanzania consider community input when displaying traditional artefacts to ensure cultural artworks are presented respectfully.
sla_exercise: What is provenance in relation to an artwork?::It is the documented history of an artwork's ownership.||Why is checking provenance important before acquiring an artwork?::It confirms the artwork was acquired legally and legitimately.||Give one ethical consideration when displaying cultural artworks.::Respecting the cultural context and involving source communities in display decisions.

sla_teaching_aids: Relevant online resources related to the archiving of artworks
sla_references: TET(2023), FINE ART SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM I-IV, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Archiving preserves artworks and their documentation for the future, while copyright law governs how archived works may be used or reproduced.
sla_notes_details: Archiving artworks involves recording detailed information about each piece, including the artist's name, title, date of creation, medium and provenance, alongside physical or digital preservation of the work itself, such as climate-controlled storage or high-resolution digital scanning. When archiving under Tanzanian copyright law, institutions must ensure that reproducing, digitising or publicly displaying archived works, particularly those still under copyright protection, is done with the permission of the copyright holder, unless the work has entered the public domain after copyright expiry.
sla_notes_illustrations: A gallery digitising a collection of paintings for a public online archive first obtains written permission from the living artists whose copyright-protected works are included.
sla_notes_daily_life: Local cultural institutions build archives of Tanzanian artists' works to preserve national artistic heritage for future generations while respecting artists' copyright.
sla_exercise: What information is typically recorded when archiving an artwork?::The artist's name, title, date of creation, medium and provenance.||Why must permission be obtained before digitising a copyrighted artwork for an archive?::Because reproducing it without permission would infringe the copyright holder's rights.||What happens to copyright protection after it expires?::The work enters the public domain and can be freely reproduced.
